full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application under section 25 of the Small Causes Court Act, 1887 and is directed against the order dated 27-8-2007 passed by the learned Assistant Judge and Small Causes Court in SCC Suit No. 31 of 1988 returning the plaint under section 23 of the Small Causes Court Act. 

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted SCC Suit No. 31 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong for eviction of the defendant-opposite parties from the shop premises as described in the schedule of the plaint and also for realization of unpaid rent. Plaintiffs' case in brief is that the suit-land on which the shop premises situated belonged to their predecessor Oli Ahmed Misri. He let out it to Bashir Ahammed, the original defendant and predecessor of the substituted defendants at monthly rent of Taka 25 payable according to Bengali month. The defendant had been paying the rent against the let out shop premises. Oli Ahmed Misri died leaving behind the plaintiffs and others. On an amicable partition of the properties left by him the plaintiffs got the shop premises in their share. After such partition of the property, the defendant had also been paying rent. At one stage the rent was enhanced to Taka 40 per month. The defendant failed to pay the rent from the month of Chaitra 1381 BS. In that event the plaintiffs filed a case before the village Court for recovery of unpaid rent to the amount of Taka 440. The case was allowed and the unpaid rent was realized through Execution Case No. 12 of 1982. Defendant again defaulted in paying the rent from the month of Chaitra, 1382 BS. 

3. The plaintiffs' further case is that the shop premises were necessary for their own purpose. They served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer Property Act dated 20-6-1996 upon the defendant and thereafter, instituted the suit for his eviction from the shop premises. 

4. The defendant was contesting the suit by filing a written statement, denying the title of the plaintiffs over the suit-land. His contention was that RS Plot No. 3212 appertaining to Khatian No. 756 under mouja Mazigao, police station Mirershorai, district Chittagong originally belonged to Ahmedur Rahman. After his death his daughter Hosneara Begum became the owner. She sold out 0.111/4 acre from said plot to Nurul Afsar and Habibur Rahman by a registered sale deed dated 16-1-1962. Habibur Rahman had erected a pucca shop on the land of his part and rented it to the defendant. He further posited that Habibur Rahman died leaving behind his one brother and two sisters as his legal heirs and successors who sold out 0.03 acre of land and the shop premises to the defendant by a sale deed dated 6-5-197. It was further stated that the plaintiffs were unsuccessful in the village Court. As he was owner of the shop premises and complicated question of title was involved in the suit, he prayed for return of the plaint under section 23 of the Small Causes Court Act. 

5. The suit was once in the peremptory hearing and the defendant having failed to appear, the suit was taken up for ex-parte hearing and after examining the plaintiffs' documents including rent-receipts, the suit was decreed by the judgment and decree dated 30-05-2000. The present defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 2001 and ultimately the said case was allowed and the SCC Suit No. 31. of 1980 was restored. Thereafter, the defendants filed an application under section 23 of Small Causes Court Act for return of the plaint and learned Senior Assistant Judge by order dated 14-5-2007 allowed the application and returned the plaint. Challenging the said order the plaintiff petitioners moved this revision and obtained the Rule. 

6. Mr Sheikh Zulfikar Bulbul Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the plaintiff petitioners instituted the suit for eviction of the defendant from the shop premises specifically stating that the defendant was a monthly tenant and that he was inducted in the shop premises by an agreement. Subsequently he became defaulter for non-payment of rent and rendered himself liable to be evicted therefrom. The claim of the defendant of acquiring title over the shop premises cannot be decided without taking evidence. The Court below only on the basis of his statement made in the written statement and in the application under section 23 of the Act and without taking the plaint and other materials produced by the plaintiffs into consideration most mechanically and arbitrarily returned the plaint. Mr Chowdhury further submits that the learned Assistant Judge without assigning any cogent reason passed the impugned order which cannot be sustained in law. 

7. In support of his submissions, Mr Chowdhury refers to the cases of Nath Ram Giridhari Ram and others vs Uttam Chand Nanak Chand, AIR 1939 Peshawar 14, Shambhu Nath Saha vs Aifazuddin Ahmed and others, 1988 BLD (AD) 270 = 41 DLR (AD) 27 and Banu Gopal Lain vs Hajee Abdul Hamid Khan and others, 2983 BLD 274. 

8. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and, perused the application and other materials on record. The present suit is for eviction of the tenant from the let out shop premises. The plaintiffs' case is that their predecessor inducted the predecessor of the present defendants into the shop premises as a monthly tenant under an agreement, and as he defaulted in paying the rent, became a defaulter and is liable to be evicted from the shop premises. It is their further case that the shop premises was necessary for their own purpose. On the other hand, the defendant in the written statement as well as in the application under section 23 of the Act claimed to have acquired title over the shop premises and tried to make out a case that a complicated question of title was involved, which could only be decided in a competent Court and in that view of the matter the plaint should be returned. 

9. In a suit brought by the land-lord for eviction of his tenant from let-out premises, the main question is whether there was an existence of relationship of land lord and tenant between the parties. On going through the plaint it is apparent that there was existence of relationship of land lord and tenant between the parties; and if that was the position it could not be said only on the basis of the claim of the defendant without taking evidence that there was no existence of such relationship. If the plaintiff by adducing evidence could be able to prove the existence of such relationship and that the tenant defaulted in paying the rent, then the plaintiffs might have succeeded in the suit. 

10. Section 23 of the Small Causes Court Act provides return of plaint in an event where plaintiffs' claim depends upon proof of title over the immovable property. This section is based on the rule of convenience. The suits triable by the Court of Small Causes are suits of simple character. When an intricate question of title is raised, that cannot be conveniently decided by such court. Therefore, the provision of return of plaint is provided there. But in order to bring a case within its scope, it must be established that the right and claim of the plaintiff depends on proof or disproof of title to immovable properly. 

11. In the present case, it is the defendant who denied the title of the plaintiffs and asserted his independent title over the shop premises. In case of proof of plaintiffs' case would disentitle him to raise his independent title over the same property in view of the provision of section 116 of the Evidence Act. In the case of Banu Gopal Lala vs Hajee Abdul Hannd Khan, 1983 BLD 274, it was held: "8. Secondly, he has sought to contend that since a complicated question of title was raised with regard to the disputed premises. The SCC Judge had no jurisdiction to try the suit under the SCC Act. The learned Advocate, however, could not point either to any provision of law or authority in support of his contention that a question as to title can never be decided in a SCC suit. Indeed section 23 of the SCC, Act gives discretion to the SCC Court to return plaint in a suit involving question of title under certain circumstances. This power is in terms discretionary and it has been held in very many cases that the section clearly indicates that a Court of Small Causes has the power to decide incidental question of title in a suit which is essentially a SCC matter. The section does not lay down that an issue as to title renders an SCC suit nonmaintainable. Be that as it may, in the instant case for eviction of a tenant, the plaintiff was not required to prove his title to the suit premises. He could prove that he had inducted Rajani Kanta Lala as his tenant, the deceased defendant and for that matter any other person in his place would be stopped from denying the title of the plaintiff under section 116 of the Evidence Act." 

12. Apart from the merit of the case, it appears from the impugned order that the learned Assistant Judge has not assigned any reason for return of the plaint. It does not transpire from the order that he has considered the case of both the parties, and after considering all the materials he has come to a conclusion that a complicated question of title is involved in the suit. The order on the face of it is a non-speaking order and on that count too the order cannot be sustained in law. 

13. Accordingly, Rule is made absolute and the impugned order dated 14-5-2007 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Sadar, Chittagong in SCC Suit No. 31 of 1988 is set-aside. 

14. Since, this is a very old case it is expedient in the interest of justice that it should be disposed of with utmost expediency, and in that view of the matter learned trial Judge is directed to dispose of the SCC suit expeditiously, preferably within six months from the date of receipt of this order without granting adjournment to the parties except on compelling reasons. 

Office is directed to send down the lower Court's record and communicate the judgment and order at once. 

End.
